{{Short description|Mathematical inequality}}
In mathematics, the '''max–min inequality''' is as follows:

:For any function <math>\ f : Z \times W \to \mathbb{R}\ ,</math>
:: <math>
\sup_{z \in Z} \inf_{w \in W} f(z, w) \leq \inf_{w \in W} \sup_{z \in Z} f(z, w)\ .
</math>

When equality holds one says that {{mvar|f}}, {{mvar|W}}, and {{mvar|Z}} satisfies a strong max–min property (or a [[saddle point|saddle-point]] property). The example function <math>\ f(z,w) = \sin( z + w )\ </math> illustrates that the equality does not hold for every function.

A theorem giving conditions on {{mvar|f}}, {{mvar|W}}, and {{mvar|Z}} which guarantee the saddle point property is called a [[minimax theorem]].

== Proof ==
Define <math> g(z) \triangleq \inf_{w \in W} f(z, w)\ .</math> For all <math>z \in Z</math>, we get  <math display="inline">g(z) \leq f(z, w) </math> for all <math>w \in W </math> by definition of the infimum being a lower bound. Next, for all <math display="inline">w \in W </math>, <math>f(z, w) \leq \sup_{z \in Z} f(z, w) </math> for all <math display="inline">z \in Z </math> by definition of the supremum being an upper bound. Thus, for all <math>z \in Z </math> and <math>w \in W </math>, <math>g(z) \leq f(z, w) \leq \sup_{z \in Z} f(z, w) </math> making <math>h(w) \triangleq \sup_{z \in Z} f(z, w) </math> an upper bound on <math>g(z) </math> for any choice of <math>w \in W </math>. Because the supremum is the least upper bound,  <math>\sup_{z \in Z} g(z) \leq h(w) </math> holds for all <math>w \in W </math>. From this inequality, we also see that <math>\sup_{z \in Z} g(z) </math> is a lower bound on <math>h(w) </math>. By the greatest lower bound property of infimum, <math>\sup_{z \in Z} g(z) \leq \inf_{w \in W} h(w) </math>. Putting all the pieces together, we get

<math>\sup_{z \in Z} \inf_{w \in W} f(z, w) = \sup_{z \in Z} g(z) \leq \inf_{w \in W} h(w) = \inf_{w \in W} \sup_{z \in Z} f(z, w) </math> 

which proves the desired inequality. <math>\blacksquare </math>
